title: Truth, lived again
hook: truth in speech and truth in conduct

segments.voice: Yesterday, prem: the heron looks holy, but only those who have loved have found the Lord. Your line was those who loved, found. Did you say the love out loud? Day one thousand three hundred ninety-nine.

On my way. A text, sent from a couch, shoes still off. Nobody would call it a lie, exactly. Nothing in the message is false in a way a court would care about. And yet something in it isn't true. The words point one direction and the person points another. This path has met sat, truth, many times: in the Mool Mantar, in the Mundavani's plate, in the Japji's opening. Today the Gurus press on the gap between the message and the couch. Truth, lived again.
screen: `ON MY WAY.` → `SENT FROM THE COUCH.` → `TRUTH, LIVED AGAIN.`

segments.voice: First, the ladder. In Sri Raag, Guru Nanak gives a short line. In the original: sachahu orai sabh ko, upar sach aachaar. In paraphrase: truth is higher than everything; higher still is truthful living. Read that slowly. Truth is at the top, and then the Guru puts one more rung above it. Not a truer idea. A truer life. Aachaar is conduct, the way a person actually behaves. Second, how truth is known. In Asa di Var, Guru Nanak gives a list, in paraphrase: one is known as true only when the truth is in the heart; then the filth of falsehood leaves, and the body is washed clean. The list goes on: when a person loves the truth, when they take true teaching, when they show compassion to living beings and give. Truth here isn't only accurate words. It's a heart and a set of habits. Third, the two kinds side by side. Truth in speech: not saying what isn't so. Truth in conduct: being what you say. A person can pass the first test all day and fail the second. On my way, sent from the couch, barely scrapes past the first and fails the second. And plenty of sentences that aren't lies at all still fail the second: I'll pray for you, never prayed. Let's get coffee, never meant. Fourth, small promises. The Guru's ladder makes the smallest promise matter. A truthful life isn't built from grand vows. It's built from returning the call you said you'd return, showing up at the time you named. Each kept promise is a rung on that ladder. Each dropped one is a little gap between the message and the couch.
screen: `TRUTH IS HIGH; TRUTHFUL LIVING IS HIGHER.` · `KNOWN TRUE WHEN THE HEART IS TRUE.` · `TRUE WORDS, AND A TRUE LIFE.` · `SMALL PROMISES ARE RUNGS.` · then, large: `UPAR SACH AACHAAR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep one small promise. Settle, and breathe. Look back over the last few days for one small thing you said you'd do and haven't. A message to answer. A book to return. A call to make. Don't scold yourself; just find it. On each breath, picture actually doing it, today, at a specific time. Then pick that time. If nothing comes to mind, make one small promise now, to yourself, that you're sure you can keep before tonight. The bell holds the time.
Truth. Sat, which the Gurus honor in speech and, higher still, in conduct: sach aachaar, a life that matches its words. Today's word.
Your line: truth in conduct. Today, keep the promise you found, at the time you picked, and say nothing about it. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-nine.

howItsDone: Sikhs hold truthful living, sach aachaar, as central to the path, and the line 'truth is high, but higher still is truthful living' from Sri Raag is quoted in Sikh teaching.

original.note: Gurmukhi: sach aachaar, truthful conduct, which Guru Nanak places above truth itself.

trapdoor: what you thought: truth means not telling lies.
what it means: the Gurus honor true words, and place a true life higher still.
what a scholar hears: Sri Raag's sachahu orai sabh ko, upar sach aachaar, and Asa di Var's list of how a person is known to be true.
